Chodel Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Chodel, Poland

Demolished. Chodel was founded in 1517 by King Sigismund the Old. From 1570, the town enforced the 'de non tolerandis Judaeis' privilege, a formal legal instrument explicitly forbidding Jews from settling or buying houses there; the earliest document confirming a Jewish tenant's residence nonetheless dates to 1746. By the second half of the 1930s, Jews made up nearly half the town's population. In May 1942, several hundred people were executed in Chodel, and the town's ghetto population was deported to Sobibór and Bełżec that same year. This cemetery, established no later than 1872, was targeted for destruction by the Germans after the 1942 deportations; its fence was dismantled after the war by Chodel's own residents, and its remains were used for construction — according to an anonymous informant, at least one private house basement is still covered with cemetery tombstones today. The site later became an illegal rubbish dump and a sand mine. In 2015, archaeological studies commissioned ahead of planned sports field construction discovered burial pits and fence-wall foundation remains, leading to the project's suspension; as of 2021, the area remains unmarked, with no form of commemoration.
